50th Anniversary of the first human heart Transplant

By: Diana Lucas | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
50th Anniversary of the first human heart transplant

Summary:
On the 3rd December 1967 South African Prof Christiaan Barnard performed the first human heart transplant at Groote Schuur hospital in Cape Town. …it was an historic moment and catapulted the Dr onto the global arena. It was 53 year old Lewis Washkansky who received the first transplant. how this has evolved woth new cutting edge, research, innovations and medicines.

In the context of the history of first human heart transplant we look at the developments that have been made since that historic operation, how this has evolved with new cutting edge, research, innovations and medicines.

We will interview one of the world’s top cardiologists Prof. John McMurray on the top advances in cardiology since the first human to human transplant. Prof. McMurray will also take us through new groundbreaking research on heart failure and a new drug that promises to reduce cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitilisation and overall quality of life by 20% each.

We will interview Kelly Perkins, hugely inspiring life story…she is the ever heart transplant recipient to reach the summits of some of the worlds most famous mountains. We will also talk to a South African heart transplant survivor.

Press Release:


50 Years of Heart Transplants
On the 3rd of December 1967, Professor Chris Barnard did the seemingly impossible - successfully
performing the world’s first heart transplant at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town and in the process,
placed the South African medical fraternity on the global map. Since that day, thousands of people have
received the gift of a new heart. Fifty years on, Carte Blanche celebrates this seminal moment in medical
history.

Script:


50th Anniversary Heart Transplant

Dini: I was called to the hospital about 10 30 on the night of the 2nd Dec 1967 it was a Saturday evening some of the sisters were arriving in their fancy dress costumes because they had been called from a party they were at, there was quiet a lot of laughing and excitement but once we changed and came into the theatre the atmosphere became very serious.

Link: 50 years ago today South African heart surgeon Christian Barnard made medical history. He successfully transplanted a human heart in to the chest cavity of 53 year old Lewis Washkansky. It was an event here at the Groote Schuur Hospital, Cape Town that catapulted him into an international celebrity.

V/O 14 sec
Dene Friedman’s role was to keep a record and regulate how the heart lung machine was performing. We met Dene at the Heart Transplant Museum at Groote Schuur and she took us back 50 years.

John: Were you aware that night of the significance of what you were involved in?
Dini: Not at all, we thought maybe in the medical world a little bit of a ripple but no body ever thought it would capture the public the way that it did.

Link: In Chris Barnard’s words it was no big deal just another heart surgery, in fact when he walked out of the operating theatre that day…there was no there, no media, no cameras, in 24 hours everything changed.

V/O 5 sec
We spoke to Chris in 1992, about his sudden celebrity status.

Chris: A man got up one…known all over the world…advise him nobody wrote that speech all those things on my own.

V/O 6 sec
Whilst the world had isolated apartheid South Africa’, Chis was adored the world over, everyone wanted to meet him……

V/O 8 sec
Prof Peter Zilla heads up the Christiaan Barnard Department for Cardiothoracic Surgery and the Cardiovascular Research Unit.

John: What was it about Chris Barnard, Cape Town and 1967 that made all the stars line up?
Prof Peter Zilla: First of all it needs a pioneer country and Europe was an old saturated country so that research towards transplantation happened in these 2 pioneer countries in the US and SA you need a certain mentality a can do mentality.

Up sound Chris “ I came to America at the time when heart surgery started and I went to the school that led the world in heart surgery”

V/O 12 sec
Chris Barnard spent 2 years in America studying at the University of Minnesota on his return to South Africa in 1958, his Professor made an offer that would change the course of medical history.

Chris Up Sound “ He called me to his office and and said Chris you are now going back to South Africa he says and you probably will need some equipment there and I said if I could just get a heart lung machine it would be terrific because I could start work straight away.

V/O 5 sec
Chris got his wish and returned with a heart lung machine, the first in the country.

Stanley: I took a decision to accept this heart a a gift from a donor and almost audibly said thank you and made peace with that and I think that was the turning point.

V/O 12 sec
In 1995 Stanley Henkeman had a massive heart attack. After six years of struggling to exercise, to breathe he received a heart transplant…he was 48 years old.

John: Do you remember the final few minutes before you were wheeled in?
Stanley: I remember it as if it was yesterday, I was lying on the bed my 2 boys were standing there and my mother and my mother had just lost her other son in an accident a few years before that and I was her only son left and to see your mother standing there in sunglasses and you know that she is struggling. I could just see on their faces deep deep anxiety.
John: It’s a story with a happy ending.?
Stanley: You know what my first recollection was when I work up not that I had a knew heart it was simply BREATHES I can breathe freely and deeply something that you cant do when you suffer from heart failure, my lungs are clean and clear and only after that it kicked in hey I am sore..

Link : The heart donor was 25 year old Denise Darvall who suffered significant brain injuries when she and her mother were knocked over by a car in Observatory by the time she was wheeled into this theatre she was brain dead.

Dini: At about quarter to 1 that evening Dr Cecil Moss brought Denise Darvall into the adjoining there and it was very sad to see this young girl lying on the operating table her black curly hair was peeping out of the bandages she looked so young she was my own age.
John: Dr Barnard on edge
Denise: I think Dr Barnard was totally confident he knew it was going to work, yes he was a bit on edge because he was walking between the two theatres saying are you ready are you ready.

V/O 16 sec
When the EEG was a flat line, Chris Barnard excised Denise’s heart himself carrying it across to his theatre in an ice cold solution, her heart was connected to the heart lung machine to keep it oxygenated… then Chris started cutting out Louis Wallansky’s diseased heart.

Dini: For me it was a very exciting evening there was a little bit of nervousness was that heart going to take over when the time came to take the patient off the heart lung machine.

V/O 8 sec
But the transplant proceeded without a hitch until finally the cross clamp was taken off the hearts aorta.

Dini ..as the oxygenated warm blood infused the heart it immediately started to quiver with life and prof B said its going to work and from the silent theatre everybody went started smiling and laughing and saying congratulations P B it was absolutely wonderful.

Link: Lewis Washkansky lived for 18 days after his transplant, whilst his heart was functioning well he contracted pneumonia and died, never leaving the hospital.

Dini: Prof B was devastated he went down to his medical rooms and cried because he felt that he had let Mr Wallansky down.

Link: One month after Washkansky’s death Chris was back in the operating theatre, the 2nd January 1968, Phillip Blaaiberg was Chris’s second heart transplant recipient the world’s third. Ten weeks after the the operation Phillip walked out of Groote Schuur and lived for a year and a half,

V/O 7 sec
Barnard’s boldness started a frenzy of heart transplant around the world. In 1968 alone around 100 heart transplants were done.

Prof Peter Zilla: The results were so bad that transplants in most of the centres was stopped this speaks for CB’s programme that even in the absence of modern immune suppression he had reasonably good results throughout the 70’s. all these surgeons who did the first 100 transplants showed that technically it’s not a big deal they died afterwards because of bad post operative immune care.

V/O 12 sec
But in 1976, the advent of cyclosporine, often called the miracle anti rejection drug, revived heart transplants around the world, giving new life to thousands (of people every year)and Chris legacy lives on.

V/O
Post Transplant Stanley rediscovered his love of athletics. He is presently chairman of the South African Transplant Association and he participated in the world Transplant games

Stanley I’ve been very fortunate to travel for my country represent my country on world stage and at the same time doing it for my donor and myself it’s the two of us doing this together.
